summary: This chapter is about understanding what a passage actually says. You will practice finding the topic and the main idea, picking out the details that support it, making sound inferences, and following written steps in the right order.

The topic is the general subject of a passage, often just a word or two. The main idea is the one point the author wants you to take away about that topic, and every supporting detail helps prove or explain it. When an answer choice is true but covers only one detail, it is usually not the main idea.

An inference is a conclusion you reach by combining clues in the text. A good inference is supported by the passage, not just possible in real life. For directions and sequences, read every step before acting and watch for order words such as first, next, then, and finally. Labels, maps, and simple charts are read the same way: check the title, the key, and the units before answering.

concepts.definition: The general subject a passage is about, usually stated in a word or short phrase, such as "sleep" or "hand washing."
concepts.tip: Ask: What is this passage about, in two or three words?

concepts.definition: The single most important point the author makes about the topic. It is often, but not always, stated in the first or last sentence of a paragraph.
concepts.tip: Topic + what the author says about it = main idea.

concepts.definition: Facts, examples, reasons, or descriptions that explain or prove the main idea. They are more specific than the main idea.
concepts.tip: If a choice is too narrow to cover the whole passage, it is a detail.

concepts.definition: A logical conclusion drawn from clues in the text when the author does not say it directly.
concepts.tip: Point to the words in the passage that back up your inference.

concepts.definition: The order in which events or steps happen. Signal words such as first, next, after, then, and finally show the order.
concepts.tip: Read all the steps before you start, then track them one by one.

concepts.definition: A short restatement of a passage's main idea and key points in your own words, leaving out minor details and personal opinions.
concepts.tip: A good summary is shorter, neutral, and covers the whole passage.

points: Answer choices that are true but cover only one part of the passage are usually details, not the main idea.
An inference must be supported by the passage; do not pick an answer just because it could be true in real life.
In step-by-step directions, a single missed or reordered step changes the final result.
When reading a label, map, or chart, check the title, key, and units first.

compare.title: Main idea vs. supporting detail
rows: Explains or proves the key point

summary: This chapter looks at how a passage is written, not just what it says. You will tell facts from opinions, figure out why the author wrote the passage and how the author feels about the subject, recognize how the text is organized, and use context to work out word meanings.

A fact can be checked and proven true or false. An opinion expresses a belief, feeling, or judgment, and often uses words such as best, should, or terrible. Authors usually write to inform, persuade, entertain, or explain, and the word choices reveal their point of view and tone.

Writers organize ideas in common patterns: sequence, cause and effect, compare and contrast, problem and solution, and description. Signal words help you spot each pattern. When you meet an unfamiliar word, use the sentence around it, such as a definition, an example, or a contrast, to make a reasonable guess.

concepts.definition: A statement that can be checked and proven true or false using evidence, such as a measurement, date, or record.
concepts.tip: If you could look it up or measure it, it is a fact.

concepts.definition: A statement of belief, feeling, or judgment that cannot be proven. Words such as best, worst, should, and beautiful often signal an opinion.
concepts.tip: Judgment words point to an opinion.

concepts.definition: The reason the author wrote the passage: to inform, to persuade, to entertain, or to explain how to do something.
concepts.tip: Ask: What does the author want the reader to do or know?

concepts.definition: The position the passage is told from (first person uses I or we; third person uses he, she, or they) and the author's attitude toward the subject.
concepts.tip: Look at the pronouns, then at the word choices.

concepts.definition: The pattern used to organize a passage, such as sequence, cause and effect, compare and contrast, problem and solution, or description.
concepts.tip: Because and as a result signal cause and effect; however and similarly signal comparison.

concepts.definition: The author's attitude as shown through word choice, such as serious, hopeful, critical, or humorous.
concepts.tip: Find two or three strong words and ask what feeling they share.

concepts.definition: Hints in nearby words or sentences, such as a definition, an example, a synonym, or a contrast, that help you figure out an unfamiliar word.
concepts.tip: Replace the hard word with your guess and reread the sentence.

points: A statement with numbers can still be an opinion if it adds a judgment, such as "the best price."
Persuasive writing takes a side and tries to change the reader's mind; informative writing stays neutral.
Signal words are the fastest way to identify text structure.
Context clues of contrast often follow words like but, however, or unlike.

compare.title: Fact vs. opinion
rows: No, it is a belief or judgment
The clinic has the friendliest staff.

summary: This chapter asks you to put information together. You will compare two or more sources, judge whether the evidence really supports a claim, combine words with charts or graphics, and choose the most trustworthy source for a task.

An argument has a claim, which is the point being argued, and evidence, which is the support for it. Strong evidence is relevant to the claim and sufficient to back it up. Watch for reasoning that jumps to a conclusion or relies only on personal feelings.

Primary sources are first-hand records made by people who were there, such as a diary, an original study, or a photograph. Secondary sources describe or interpret primary sources, such as a textbook or a news analysis. When choosing a source, look at who wrote it, how current it is, and whether the author has a reason to be biased.

concepts.definition: The main point or position an author is trying to prove in an argument.
concepts.tip: The claim is what the author wants you to believe.

concepts.definition: Facts, data, examples, or expert statements used to support a claim. Good evidence is relevant (on topic) and sufficient (enough of it).
concepts.tip: Relevant and sufficient: both are needed.

concepts.definition: An original, first-hand record created at the time by someone directly involved, such as a letter, diary, interview, original research report, or photograph.
concepts.tip: Primary = I was there.

concepts.definition: A source that describes, summarizes, or interprets primary sources, such as a textbook, encyclopedia article, or review.
concepts.tip: Secondary = someone telling you about it later.

concepts.definition: A one-sided leaning that can make a source unfair or incomplete, often because the author benefits from a certain conclusion.
concepts.tip: Ask: Who gains if I believe this?

concepts.definition: A source you can reasonably trust because it is written by a qualified author, is current, cites evidence, and comes from a reputable publisher or organization.
concepts.tip: Check author, date, evidence, and publisher.

points: When two sources disagree, compare their evidence, not just their conclusions.
A single personal story is weak evidence for a broad claim.
For up-to-date health or science facts, a recent source from an expert organization beats an old or anonymous one.
When a passage includes a chart, the correct answer must agree with both the text and the chart.

compare.title: Primary vs. secondary source
rows: Someone looking back at the event or data
At the time of the event or study

summary: This chapter covers the number skills used in everyday math: fractions, decimals, and percents, ordering numbers, ratios and proportions, and solving simple equations and inequalities. Many questions are word problems, so turning sentences into math is a key skill.

Fractions, decimals, and percents are three ways to write the same amount. To change a fraction to a decimal, divide the top by the bottom; to change a decimal to a percent, multiply by 100. When solving a problem with several operations, follow the order of operations: parentheses, exponents, multiplication and division from left to right, then addition and subtraction from left to right.

A ratio compares two amounts, and a proportion says two ratios are equal. You can solve a proportion by cross-multiplying. To solve an equation, do the same operation to both sides until the variable is alone. Inequalities work the same way, except that multiplying or dividing both sides by a negative number flips the inequality sign.

concepts.definition: Three forms of the same value. Divide numerator by denominator to get a decimal, then multiply by 100 to get a percent. Example: 3/4 = 0.75 = 75%.
concepts.tip: Percent means per hundred.

concepts.definition: The agreed order for solving expressions: parentheses, exponents, multiplication and division (left to right), then addition and subtraction (left to right).
concepts.tip: PEMDAS, but do multiply/divide and add/subtract left to right.

concepts.definition: A comparison of two quantities, written as 3:4, 3 to 4, or 3/4.
concepts.tip: Keep the order of the words in the order of the numbers.

concepts.definition: An equation stating that two ratios are equal, such as 2/5 = x/20. Solve by cross-multiplying: 2 x 20 = 5x, so x = 8.
concepts.tip: Line up matching units on top and bottom before you cross-multiply.

concepts.definition: How much an amount went up or down compared with where it started: (new - original) / original x 100.
concepts.tip: Always divide by the original amount.

concepts.definition: Getting the variable alone by doing inverse operations to both sides. Example: 3x + 4 = 19, subtract 4 to get 3x = 15, divide by 3 to get x = 5.
concepts.tip: Undo addition or subtraction first, then multiplication or division.

concepts.definition: When you multiply or divide both sides of an inequality by a negative number, the sign reverses. Example: -2x > 6 becomes x < -3.
concepts.tip: Negative multiply or divide = flip the sign.

points: To compare fractions, decimals, and percents, change them all to decimals first.
"Of" in a percent problem usually means multiply: 20% of 50 = 0.20 x 50 = 10.
Check an equation's answer by putting it back into the original equation.
In word problems, "is" usually means equals, and "more than" means add.

summary: This chapter covers measuring and describing things with numbers. You will read tables and graphs, find the mean, median, mode, and range of a data set, spot outliers, convert between U.S. customary and metric units, and find perimeter, area, and volume of basic shapes.

The mean is the average: add all the values and divide by how many there are. The median is the middle value after the data are put in order, and the mode is the value that appears most often. For the data 2, 3, 3, 4, 8, the mean is 20 divided by 5, which is 4, while the median and the mode are both 3. The single high value of 8 is an outlier, and it pulls the mean up but barely moves the median, while the range (highest value minus lowest) shows how spread out the data are.

For unit conversions, multiply by a conversion factor so that the unwanted unit cancels out. Common factors include 1 inch = 2.54 centimeters, 1 kilogram is about 2.2 pounds, and 1 liter = 1,000 milliliters. Perimeter is the distance around a shape, area is the space it covers in square units, and volume is the space it fills in cubic units.

concepts.definition: The average of a data set: add all the values and divide by the number of values. For 2, 3, 3, 4, 8 the mean is 20 / 5 = 4.
concepts.tip: Mean = sum / count. Outliers pull it toward them.

concepts.definition: The middle value when the data are in order. With an even number of values, it is the mean of the two middle values. For 2, 3, 3, 4, 8 the median is 3.
concepts.tip: Sort first, then find the middle.

concepts.definition: The value that appears most often. A data set can have no mode, one mode, or more than one. For 2, 3, 3, 4, 8 the mode is 3.
concepts.tip: Mode = most often.

concepts.definition: The difference between the largest and smallest values, showing how spread out the data are. For 2, 3, 3, 4, 8 the range is 8 - 2 = 6.
concepts.tip: Range = max - min.

concepts.definition: A value far away from the rest of the data. An outlier pulls the mean toward it but has little effect on the median.
concepts.tip: With an outlier, the median describes the typical value better.

concepts.definition: Exact or standard factors: 1 inch = 2.54 cm, 1 kg is about 2.2 lb, 1 L = 1,000 mL, 1 kg = 1,000 g, 1 m = 100 cm.
concepts.tip: Set up the factor so the unit you want to remove cancels.

concepts.definition: Perimeter is the distance around a shape (rectangle: 2l + 2w). Area is the surface covered (rectangle: l x w; circle: pi x r squared). Volume is the space inside (box: l x w x h).
concepts.tip: Perimeter in units, area in square units, volume in cubic units.

points: Always sort the data before finding the median.
One very high or very low value changes the mean much more than the median.
When converting from a larger unit to a smaller one, the number gets bigger (2 m = 200 cm).
Read graph titles, axis labels, and scales before choosing an answer.

compare.title: Mean, median, and mode
rows: Add all values, divide by the count

figures.alt: Dot plot on a number line from 0 to 10 showing 2, 3, 3, 4, 8, with two dots stacked at 3. A triangle under 3 is labeled Median = 3 and one under 4 is labeled Mean = 4. The dot at 8 is labeled Outlier. Text above: Mean = 20 ÷ 5 = 4, Median = 3, Mode = 3.
figures.caption: For 2, 3, 3, 4, 8, the median (middle value) is 3, but one high outlier (8) pulls the mean up to 4.

summary: This chapter covers how the human body is organized and how its major systems work together. You will learn directional terms, the path of blood and air, how food is digested, how nerves and hormones send signals, and how the body keeps itself in balance.

The body is organized from cells to tissues to organs to organ systems. Directional terms describe location: superior means toward the head, inferior means toward the feet, anterior means front, posterior means back, medial means toward the midline, and lateral means away from it. Proximal and distal describe a limb, meaning closer to or farther from where it attaches to the trunk.

In the heart, oxygen-poor blood enters the right atrium, moves to the right ventricle, and is pumped to the lungs. Oxygen-rich blood returns to the left atrium, moves to the left ventricle, and leaves through the aorta to the body. In the lungs, oxygen and carbon dioxide are exchanged in tiny air sacs called alveoli. Most digestion and absorption of nutrients happen in the small intestine.

The nervous system sends fast electrical signals, while the endocrine system sends slower chemical signals called hormones through the blood. Both help maintain homeostasis, the body's effort to keep conditions such as temperature and blood sugar stable. Most of this control uses negative feedback, where a change triggers a response that brings things back toward normal.

concepts.definition: The body's ability to keep internal conditions, such as temperature, blood sugar, and fluid balance, within a stable range.
concepts.tip: Homeo = same, stasis = standing still.

concepts.definition: A control loop in which a change triggers a response that reverses it, such as sweating when body temperature rises. Most homeostatic control works this way.
concepts.tip: Negative feedback pushes back toward normal.

concepts.definition: Superior (toward the head) vs. inferior (toward the feet); anterior (front) vs. posterior (back); medial (toward the midline) vs. lateral (away from it); proximal (closer to the trunk) vs. distal (farther).
concepts.tip: Distal = distant from the trunk.

concepts.definition: Body -> vena cavae -> right atrium -> right ventricle -> pulmonary artery -> lungs -> pulmonary veins -> left atrium -> left ventricle -> aorta -> body.
concepts.tip: Right side to the lungs, left side to the body.

concepts.definition: Arteries carry blood away from the heart; veins carry blood back to the heart. The pulmonary arteries are the exception that carries oxygen-poor blood.
concepts.tip: Arteries = away.

concepts.definition: Tiny air sacs in the lungs, surrounded by capillaries, where oxygen passes into the blood and carbon dioxide passes out.
concepts.tip: Alveoli are where gas exchange happens.

concepts.definition: The nervous system uses electrical impulses along neurons for fast, short responses. The endocrine system uses hormones carried in the blood for slower, longer-lasting effects.
concepts.tip: Nerves = fast wires; hormones = slow mail.

points: The left ventricle has the thickest wall because it pumps blood to the whole body.
Most nutrient absorption happens in the small intestine; the large intestine mainly absorbs water.
The kidneys filter blood and make urine, which flows through the ureters to the bladder.
Insulin from the pancreas lowers blood sugar; glucagon raises it.
Red blood cells carry oxygen, white blood cells fight infection, and platelets help blood clot.

summary: This chapter covers life at the level of the cell. You will learn the parts of a cell and what they do, how cells divide, how DNA carries instructions to make proteins, how traits are passed from parents to children, and the basic types of microorganisms.

Each organelle has a job. The nucleus holds the DNA, mitochondria make most of the cell's energy in the form of ATP, ribosomes build proteins, and the cell membrane controls what goes in and out. Plant cells also have a cell wall and chloroplasts for photosynthesis.

Mitosis makes two identical body cells for growth and repair, while meiosis makes four sex cells, each with half the usual number of chromosomes. DNA is copied into RNA in a step called transcription, and RNA is used to build a protein in a step called translation. In genetics, a dominant allele shows its trait even if only one copy is present, while a recessive trait shows only when both copies are recessive.

concepts.definition: Organelles that carry out cellular respiration and produce most of the cell's usable energy as ATP.
concepts.tip: Mitochondria = the cell's power plant.

concepts.definition: The nucleus stores DNA and controls the cell. Ribosomes read RNA instructions and assemble proteins from amino acids.
concepts.tip: Nucleus holds the plans; ribosomes build the product.

concepts.definition: Cell division that produces two daughter cells identical to the parent, each with the full set of chromosomes. Used for growth and repair.
concepts.tip: Mitosis: 2 identical cells.

concepts.definition: Cell division that produces four sex cells (eggs or sperm), each with half the chromosomes of the parent cell, and genetically different from one another.
concepts.tip: Meiosis: 4 cells, half the chromosomes.

concepts.definition: Transcription copies a gene from DNA into messenger RNA in the nucleus. Translation uses that RNA at a ribosome to build a protein.
concepts.tip: DNA -> RNA -> protein.

concepts.definition: In DNA, adenine pairs with thymine and cytosine pairs with guanine. In RNA, uracil replaces thymine, so adenine pairs with uracil.
concepts.tip: A-T and C-G in DNA; A-U in RNA.

concepts.definition: A dominant allele shows its trait with just one copy. A recessive trait shows only when both alleles are recessive. A Punnett square predicts offspring combinations.
concepts.tip: Aa x Aa gives a 3:1 ratio of dominant to recessive traits.

points: Bacteria are prokaryotes with no nucleus; human, plant, and fungal cells are eukaryotes with a nucleus.
Viruses are not cells and need a host cell to reproduce.
Homozygous means two matching alleles (AA or aa); heterozygous means two different alleles (Aa).
Human body cells have 46 chromosomes; sex cells have 23.

summary: This chapter covers the basics of matter and how it changes. You will learn the parts of an atom, how the periodic table is arranged, how atoms bond, the states of matter, how to balance a chemical equation, and how acids, bases, and solutions behave.

An atom has protons and neutrons in its nucleus and electrons around it. The atomic number is the number of protons, which decides which element it is, and the mass number is protons plus neutrons. Atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons are called isotopes. Ionic bonds form when electrons are transferred, usually between a metal and a nonmetal, while covalent bonds form when electrons are shared, usually between nonmetals.

A balanced chemical equation has the same number of each kind of atom on both sides, because matter is not created or destroyed. The pH scale runs from 0 to 14: below 7 is acidic, 7 is neutral, and above 7 is basic. In a solution, the solute is the substance being dissolved and the solvent is the substance doing the dissolving.

concepts.definition: Protons (positive) and neutrons (no charge) sit in the nucleus; electrons (negative) move around it. A neutral atom has equal numbers of protons and electrons.
concepts.tip: Protons positive, neutrons neutral, electrons negative.

concepts.definition: Atomic number = number of protons and identifies the element. Mass number = protons + neutrons. Neutrons = mass number - atomic number.
concepts.tip: Change the protons and you change the element.

concepts.definition: Atoms of the same element (same number of protons) with different numbers of neutrons, so they have different mass numbers.
concepts.tip: Isotopes: same protons, different neutrons.

concepts.definition: An ionic bond forms when one atom gives electrons to another, usually metal to nonmetal. A covalent bond forms when atoms share electrons, usually between nonmetals.
concepts.tip: Ionic = give and take; covalent = share.

concepts.definition: Adjusting the coefficients in front of formulas so each element has the same number of atoms on both sides. Example: 2H2 + O2 -> 2H2O.
concepts.tip: Change coefficients, never subscripts.

concepts.definition: A 0 to 14 scale of how acidic or basic a solution is. Below 7 is acidic, 7 is neutral (pure water), and above 7 is basic.
concepts.tip: Lower pH = more acidic.

concepts.definition: In a solution, the solute is the substance dissolved (such as salt) and the solvent is what it dissolves in (such as water).
concepts.tip: The solvent does the dissolving.

points: Elements in the same column (group) of the periodic table have similar chemical properties.
Melting, freezing, and boiling are physical changes; burning and rusting are chemical changes.
In a balanced equation, total mass of reactants equals total mass of products.
Acids release hydrogen ions (H+) in water; bases release hydroxide ions (OH-) or accept H+.

summary: This chapter covers how scientists ask and answer questions. You will learn the steps of an investigation, the different types of variables, how to write a testable hypothesis, which tools and units to use for measurements, and how to draw fair conclusions from data.

An investigation usually starts with an observation and a question, followed by a hypothesis, an experiment, data collection, analysis, and a conclusion. The independent variable is what the scientist changes on purpose, the dependent variable is what is measured, and controlled variables are kept the same so the test is fair. A control group receives no treatment so the results can be compared.

Choose tools that match what you measure: a balance for mass, a graduated cylinder for liquid volume, a thermometer for temperature. A conclusion should come only from the data collected and should say whether the data support the hypothesis. Correlation, where two things change together, does not by itself prove that one causes the other.

concepts.definition: A testable prediction that answers a research question, often written as an if-then statement.
concepts.tip: If I change X, then Y will happen.

concepts.definition: The factor the scientist deliberately changes to see its effect. It is usually plotted on the x-axis of a graph.
concepts.tip: I change the independent variable.

concepts.definition: The factor that is measured to see how it responds to the independent variable. It is usually plotted on the y-axis.
concepts.tip: The dependent variable depends on the change.

concepts.definition: Conditions kept the same across all trials so that only the independent variable could cause a difference.
concepts.tip: Controlled = kept constant.

concepts.definition: The group in an experiment that does not receive the treatment and serves as a baseline for comparison.
concepts.tip: The control group shows what happens without the change.

concepts.definition: Correlation means two things change together. Causation means one actually causes the other. A controlled experiment is needed to show causation.
concepts.tip: Together does not mean because.

points: Repeating trials and using larger samples makes results more reliable.
A hypothesis that the data do not support is still a valid result; it is rejected, not hidden.
Use a balance for mass (grams), a graduated cylinder for liquid volume (milliliters), and a thermometer for temperature (degrees Celsius).
A theory is a well-tested explanation; a law describes what happens, often as a formula.

summary: This chapter covers the rules that make writing correct and easy to read: spelling, punctuation, capitalization, and complete sentences. Questions usually ask you to find an error or choose the correctly punctuated sentence.

A complete sentence, or independent clause, has a subject, a verb, and a complete thought. A fragment is missing one of these. A run-on sentence joins two independent clauses with no punctuation, and a comma splice joins them with only a comma. You can fix either with a period, a semicolon, or a comma followed by a coordinating conjunction such as and, but, or so.

Commas separate items in a list, follow an introductory phrase, and set off extra information. Apostrophes show possession or replace missing letters in contractions, but they never make a word plural. Capitalize proper nouns, the first word of a sentence, and titles used before a name.

concepts.definition: A group of words punctuated as a sentence but missing a subject, a verb, or a complete thought. Example: "Because the clinic was closed."
concepts.tip: Ask: Could this stand alone and make sense?

concepts.definition: A run-on joins two complete sentences with no punctuation. A comma splice joins them with only a comma. Both are errors.
concepts.tip: Two full sentences need more than a comma.

concepts.definition: Joins two closely related complete sentences without a conjunction, and separates list items that already contain commas.
concepts.tip: A semicolon works where a period would also work.

concepts.definition: Use a comma before a coordinating conjunction (for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so) when it joins two complete sentences.
concepts.tip: FANBOYS: comma + conjunction joins two sentences.

concepts.definition: Shows ownership (the nurse's chart, the nurses' station) or replaces missing letters (do not = don't). Never use it to make a simple plural.
concepts.tip: It's = it is; its = belonging to it.

concepts.definition: Capitalize the first word of a sentence, proper nouns (specific names of people, places, organizations, days, months), and titles directly before a name.
concepts.tip: Specific name = capital; general word = lowercase.

points: Singular possessive adds 's (the patient's room); plural ending in s adds only ' (the patients' rooms).
Seasons (spring, winter) are not capitalized unless they start a sentence.
Commonly confused words: their/there/they're, your/you're, affect (verb)/effect (noun).
Periods and commas go inside closing quotation marks in American English.

compare.title: Fixing two complete sentences
rows: The shift ended. Maria went home.
The shift ended; Maria went home.
The shift ended, so Maria went home.
The shift ended, Maria went home.

summary: This chapter covers using grammar correctly in real writing. You will make subjects agree with verbs and pronouns agree with the nouns they replace, keep verb tenses consistent, and choose a style that fits the audience.

A singular subject takes a singular verb and a plural subject takes a plural verb, even when words come between them. Subjects joined by and are usually plural, and words such as each, everyone, and nobody are singular. A pronoun must match its antecedent, the noun it refers to, in number and person, and it should be clear which noun it means.

Keep the verb tense the same unless the time of the action really changes. Formal writing, such as a report or a letter to a school, avoids slang, contractions, and overly casual phrases. Clear writing is also concise: it cuts repeated words and uses the active voice when possible.

concepts.definition: The verb must match its subject in number. Ignore phrases between them: "The box of gloves is on the shelf" (box is singular).
concepts.tip: Cross out the prepositional phrase, then match the verb.

concepts.definition: Words such as each, every, everyone, either, neither, and nobody are singular and take singular verbs: "Each of the nurses has a badge."
concepts.tip: Words ending in -one or -body are singular.

concepts.definition: A pronoun must match the noun it replaces in number and person, and it must be clear which noun it refers to.
concepts.tip: Find the noun first, then pick the pronoun.

concepts.definition: Keep all verbs in the same tense (past, present, or future) unless the time of the action actually changes.
concepts.tip: Do not switch from past to present in the middle of a story.

concepts.definition: Formal style uses complete sentences, precise words, and no slang or contractions. Informal style is conversational and fits personal messages.
concepts.tip: For school, work, and reports, choose formal.

concepts.definition: In active voice the subject does the action ("The nurse checked the chart"). In passive voice the subject receives it ("The chart was checked by the nurse").
concepts.tip: Active voice is usually clearer and shorter.

points: Two subjects joined by and take a plural verb; with or or nor, the verb matches the closer subject.
Collective nouns such as team or staff usually take a singular verb when acting as one group.
Avoid vague pronouns: if "it" or "they" could mean two things, name the noun.
Concise writing removes repeated ideas, such as "past history" or "end result."

compare.title: Formal vs. informal wording
rows: I can't make it to class.
I am unable to attend class.

summary: This chapter covers how to figure out word meanings and how to organize writing clearly. You will use context clues and word parts, such as prefixes, roots, and suffixes, and you will learn how topic sentences, supporting details, and transitions hold a paragraph together.

Many English words, especially medical and science terms, are built from Greek and Latin parts. A prefix comes at the start and changes the meaning, a root carries the core meaning, and a suffix comes at the end and often shows the part of speech. For example, hypo- means under and hyper- means over, so hypothermia is low body temperature and hyperthermia is high body temperature.

A well-organized paragraph starts with a topic sentence that states its main point, follows with supporting details, and ends with a closing sentence. Transition words guide the reader: however and on the other hand show contrast, therefore and as a result show cause and effect, and first, next, and finally show order. Choosing the right transition makes the relationship between ideas clear.

concepts.definition: A word part added to the beginning of a root that changes its meaning. Examples: pre- (before), post- (after), anti- (against), un- (not).
concepts.tip: Break the word apart and translate each piece.

concepts.definition: The main part of a word that carries its core meaning. Examples: cardi (heart), derm (skin), neur (nerve), gastr (stomach).
concepts.tip: Learn common body-part roots for health words.

concepts.definition: A word part added to the end of a word that changes its meaning or part of speech. Examples: -itis (inflammation), -ology (study of), -less (without).
concepts.tip: The suffix often tells you what kind of word it is.

concepts.definition: Hypo- means under, below, or less than normal (hypoglycemia = low blood sugar). Hyper- means over, above, or more than normal (hypertension = high blood pressure).
concepts.tip: Hypo is low; hyper is high.

concepts.definition: The sentence, usually first in a paragraph, that states the paragraph's main point. Every other sentence in the paragraph should support it.
concepts.tip: If a sentence does not support the topic sentence, it does not belong.

concepts.definition: Words and phrases that show how ideas connect: contrast (however, although), cause and effect (therefore, as a result), addition (also, furthermore), order (first, finally).
concepts.tip: Name the relationship first, then pick the transition.

points: Denotation is a word's dictionary meaning; connotation is the feeling it carries (thrifty vs. cheap).
Context clues can confirm or correct a guess based on word parts.
"However" and "therefore" connect ideas with opposite logic: contrast vs. result.
A strong paragraph stays on one main idea from start to finish.

compare.title: Common transitions by purpose
